rv.q: Those politics make “What Became of Us” a highly topical play, if a frustrating one in Jennifer Chang’s production for Atlantic Theater Company.
Every design element contributes to the forward motion of the story, never drawing focus from the excellent performances of the two actors.
As he has done with Purlie Victorious and A Soldier’s Play , director Kenny Leon rescues another neglected, vital work of the African-American theatrical canon with a fresh, exciting production.
What gives the play its special fillip is the fact that Q, seven years older than her brother, was born in an unspecified "Old Country" and is, along with their parents, an immigrant.

What Became of Us is a beautiful meditation on the life and offers up a unique theatregoing experience with its double casting, but the heightened language and lack of dialogue exchange slow the pace.
But the production is also shot through with several unusual choices, which I found alternately innovative and undermining; sometimes just baffling.
What mitigates the play’s sense of detachment and lends some charm to its familiar story is the anonymity of those blank specifics regarding places of origin and residence.
I wish I could report that it was a resounding success.

cn.t: A modest, moving sibling drama about immigrant children earns praise for tender performances and poignant moments, though critics are divided on its unconventional storytelling choices and deliberately sparse, universalized approach.

vr.q: The story felt kind of surface level to me and I thought the last third of it was more or less a series of cliches.
